title: Turnvater: Lanz to Freyburg, the Body Made a Fatherland
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: Das Kind der Prignitz: The Pastor's Son (1778–1794)

stops.name: Lanz, the parsonage in the Prignitz
stops.campa: In the flat sandy country of the Prignitz, in the little village of Lanz, on 11 August 1778 the pastor's wife bears a son, Friedrich Ludwig Christoph Jahn. The father tends a scattered flock of peasants; the boy grows barefoot among horses, ponds and pine, running the heath, wrestling the village children. He learns his letters at his father's knee and his defiance in the open field. Already the child cannot bear to sit still indoors. The Mark that raised the Prussian kings raises the man who will teach Germans to leap.
suggested_refs: Jahn birth-house at Lanz (Jahn memorial site)

stops.name: Salzwedel, the Gymnasium of the Altmark
stops.campa: The boy is sent across the Elbe to the old Hanseatic town of Salzwedel, to sit at last in a Latin schoolroom. The confinement galls him. He chafes at the pedantry of grammar drilled by rote and at masters who prize the dead tongues over living limbs. Yet here he begins to gather the German words the schools despise, hoarding old and dialect speech like a miser. The seed of the language-purist is planted in the very rooms that would breed it out of him.

stops.name: Berlin, the Graues Kloster and the first flight
stops.campa: At the Gymnasium zum Grauen Kloster in Berlin the restless youth is enrolled and does not stay. He quarrels with the discipline of the cloister-school and leaves without his leaving-certificate, the first of many partings. Berlin, the capital he will one day fill with vaulting boys, first knows him as a truant. He wanders home, half-schooled, wholly ungovernable: a young man who will take no degree the ordinary way and yet be called Father by tens of thousands.

stops.name: Halle, matriculation in theology
stops.campa: At the University of Halle Jahn matriculates in theology in the autumn of 1796. He reads little scripture and much German history; he brawls, roves, and offends the authorities. In 1800 a Leipzig affair goes against him and he is banned from the German universities: a sentence he answers by studying anyway, under other names, in other towns. The pattern of his life is already set: forbidden and unstoppable, expelled and returning, a man the state cannot keep in any room it builds.

stops.name: Greifswald, the meeting with Arndt
stops.campa: In Swedish Pomerania, at Greifswald, Jahn falls in with Ernst Moritz Arndt, and the loose fire in him takes a shape. From Arndt he catches the two passions of his life: hatred of foreign rule over Germans and love of the mother-tongue purged of French. He tramps the Baltic shore and the inland roads, sleeping in barns, marking how the common people speak, work, and hold their bodies. The vagabond is becoming a prophet of the Volk, gathering his gospel not from books but from the walking of the land.

stops.name: Neubrandenburg, tutor in Mecklenburg
stops.campa: For his bread Jahn becomes a house-tutor to the children of Baron von le Fort near Neubrandenburg. He teaches, but more than teaching he leads the young outdoors: hikes across the Mecklenburg lakes, games, swimming in cold water, running until the lungs burn. Here, in the plainest of employments, he first practises what the Hasenheide will one day proclaim: that the schooling of a people begins in the free use of its limbs under the open sky. The tutor is drafting the Turnplatz in the fields.

stops.name: Göttingen, the last lecture-halls
stops.campa: At Göttingen Jahn returns to the university benches he can never quite leave nor finish. Across thirteen semesters in many towns he has heard philology, history, philosophy, and taken no degree. He is thirty and unplaced, a scholar without a chair, a patriot without a country that yet exists. Then the earth moves under all such private failures: Napoleon's armies gather on the German lands, and the roving student's small griefs are about to be swallowed in a national catastrophe that will make him.

stops.name: Jena, the field of the great shame
stops.campa: On 14 October 1806, on the plateau above Jena and at Auerstedt, Napoleon shatters the army of Frederick the Great in a single day. Jahn, serving as courier, sees the proud Prussian state broken like glass, its fortresses surrendering without a shot, its king in flight. The shame enters him like iron. In that ruin he takes the vow that governs the rest of his life: to work for the unity and freedom of Germany, and to forge a generation of bodies hard enough that such a day can never come again.
stops.quote: for the unity and freedom of Germany
stops.quote_source: Jahn's lifelong resolve after Jena, as recorded by the Friedrich-Ludwig-Jahn-Museum

stops.name: Schnepfenthal, at the feet of GutsMuths
stops.campa: Jahn journeys to Schnepfenthal in the Thuringian hills, to the school of Johann Christoph Friedrich GutsMuths, the quiet master who first wrote gymnastics for the young. He watches the exercises, weighs the apparatus, learns the grammar of the leaping body. But where GutsMuths teaches health, Jahn will teach nation; where the elder man builds strong pupils, the younger will build soldiers of a Germany not yet born. He takes the method and sets it on fire with a purpose the schoolmaster never dreamed.

segments.name: Volkstum: The Word and the Plan (1809–1810)

stops.name: Berlin, the Plamann School and the Grey Cloister
stops.campa: Jahn comes to Berlin in 1809 and takes work teaching at the Plamann boarding-school and at the Gymnasium zum Grauen Kloster, the very cloister from which he once fled as a boy. He gathers pupils and leads them out of the classroom on free afternoons: to the fields south of the city they walk, to run, wrestle and vault. Word passes among the boys of a strange master who thinks the body a school and the meadow a temple. Around him, almost by accident, a movement begins to breathe.

stops.name: Lübeck, Deutsches Volkstum goes to press
stops.campa: In 1810 Jahn's book Deutsches Volkstum is printed at Lübeck, and with it he gives the German language a new word for the soul of a people. Volkstum, he writes, is the common element of the folk, its inward essence, its stirring and its life, its power to renew and beget itself. A Germany carved into three hundred princedoms, occupied and humiliated, is told it possesses one thing no conqueror can seize: its own peoplehood. The manifesto of the coming nation is set in type while French garrisons still hold the roads.
stops.quote: Volkstum ist das Gemeinsame des Volkes, sein inwohnendes Wesen, sein Regen und Leben, seine Wiedererzeugungskraft.

stops.name: Berlin, Hasenheide: the founding of the Turnplatz
stops.campa: On 19 June 1811, on the sandy heath called the Hasenheide south of Berlin, Jahn opens the first Turnplatz, the first open-air gymnasium of the German people. He sets up bars and beam, rings and vaulting-buck, and the youth come to run, leap, climb and throw in the free air, in sight of all, without rank or fee. This is reckoned the birth-hour of the whole gymnastic movement: the body made public, made national, made ready. Here the word Turnen itself is coined and given to the German tongue.

stops.name: Berlin, the Berliner Turnverein and the Turnfahrten
stops.campa: From the Hasenheide the thing spreads like wildfire. Jahn founds the Berliner Turnverein and leads the Turnfahrten: long marches into the country, hundreds of boys tramping in grey linen, singing, sleeping under the sky, camping like an army in training. To the fearful eyes of princes it looks like a secret host being raised; to Jahn it is exactly that. By the war's coming his gymnasts number in the hundreds, a brotherhood bound by the four words he gives them: frisch, fromm, fröhlich, frei.
stops.quote_source: Jahn's Turner motto, the four F's (Turnerkreuz)

segments.name: Lützows wilde Jagd: The War of Liberation (1813–1815)

stops.name: Breslau, the muster of the Free Corps
stops.campa: When Prussia rises at last against Napoleon in the spring of 1813, Jahn shuts the Turnplatz and marches. At Breslau the volunteer Free Corps of Major von Lützow is formed, and Jahn takes it up, leading a body of his older gymnasts into its ranks. Into the same black-clad corps come the poet Theodor Körner, the Turner Friesen, and the young Friedrich Fröbel, who leaves his crystals and his children's schoolroom to shoulder a musket. The Turnplatz has become an army; the training was always for this.
suggested_refs: Lützow Free Corps in black uniform

stops.name: Gadebusch, the wood where Körner falls
stops.campa: On 26 August 1813, in the wood of Rosenow near Gadebusch, the Lützowers clash with the enemy and the poet Theodor Körner is struck down, dying that same day with his sword-and-lyre songs unfinished. The corps that owes half its fame to his verse now owes it a martyr. Jahn marches on through the campaign with his gymnasts, the men he made strong on the Hasenheide now proving in blood what the leaping and vaulting were for. Lützow's wild hunt rides across the German north.
stops.quote: Das war Lützows wilde verwegene Jagd.

stops.name: The Göhrde, the charge and the maiden-soldier
stops.campa: On 16 September 1813 the Lützow corps fights at the Göhrde forest under Wallmoden, breaking French columns among the trees. Here Eleonore Prochaska, who marched disguised as the jäger August Renz, is torn by grapeshot carrying a wounded comrade from the line; only as her wounds are dressed is her sex discovered. She dies weeks later at Dannenberg, the maiden who bore arms for Germany. Around her the corps of gymnasts, poets and painters bleeds and holds: the flower of the awakening nation, forged and spent in a season.

stops.name: Leipzig, the Battle of the Nations
stops.campa: From 16 to 19 October 1813, on the fields around Leipzig, half a million men decide the fate of Europe in the Battle of the Nations, and Napoleon is broken and driven back over the Rhine. Jahn stands with the victory that answers, at last, the shame he swore upon at Jena seven years before. The bodies he trained have helped to free the fatherland. The Turnvater has kept his vow in arms; now he means to keep it in peace, raising a whole nation of such bodies for the Germany that must be made.

segments.name: Turnkunst und Burschenschaft: Master and Kindler (1815–1817)

stops.name: Jena, the birth of the Urburschenschaft
stops.campa: On 12 June 1815 at Jena the returned volunteers found the first Burschenschaft, the German student brotherhood, in the colours black-red-gold that will one day be the nation's flag. Jahn's spirit is in it: his gymnasts and Lützowers are its founders, his gospel of one free Germany its creed. From the Turnplatz to the fraternity the same fire runs. The princes, restored and frightened, watch the students and the Turners with the same narrowing eye, sensing in this youth a power that means to unmake the map they have just redrawn.

stops.name: Berlin, Die Deutsche Turnkunst printed
stops.campa: In 1816 Jahn, with Ernst Eiselen, brings out Die Deutsche Turnkunst, the book that gives the movement its law. In it he sets down the apparatus and the exercises: the horse, the bars, the high bar, the vault; and the whole German tongue of Turnen he has forged, word by word, so that the leaping body might speak its own language. The laboriously rediscovered and awakened German gymnastic art, he writes, must not be marred by half-knowing. The scattered clubs now hold a single code; the master has written the scripture of the Turnplatz.
stops.quote: die mühsam wiedergefundene und erweckte deutsche Turnkunst
stops.quote_source: Friedrich Ludwig Jahn & Ernst Eiselen, Die Deutsche Turnkunst, Vorbericht (Berlin, 1816)

stops.name: Eisenach, the Wartburg: the students' fire
stops.campa: On 18 October 1817, on the fourth anniversary of Leipzig and the third centenary of Luther's theses, the Burschenschaften climb the Wartburg above Eisenach and light a great bonfire. As the songs and speeches rise, Jahn's men fling upon the flames mock-titles of reactionary books and the emblems of the old order: a corporal's cane, a Hessian pigtail-wig. Jahn is not present, yet the deed is laid at his door; the frightened courts read in the smoke of the Wartburg the shape of the demagogue they will now hunt. The reckoning is prepared.

segments.name: Die Turnsperre: The Ban and the Fortress (1819–1825)

stops.name: Berlin, the Turnplatz closed, the man taken
stops.campa: In March 1819 the student Karl Sand stabs the playwright Kotzebue, and the shot gives the princes their pretext. The Hasenheide is padlocked, the Turnen forbidden across the German lands: the Turnsperre that will bind the gymnasts for more than twenty years. On 13 July 1819 Jahn himself is arrested in Berlin as a demagogue, a stirrer of dangerous youth. The Father of Gymnastics, who freed his body for a fatherland, is marched off to prison by the very state whose armies he helped to victory. The open air is taken from him.

stops.name: Küstrin, the fortress on the Oder
stops.campa: From the Spandau citadel Jahn is moved to the fortress of Küstrin on the Oder, held while the courts pick over his words and his marches for treason they cannot quite find. He is questioned, transferred, kept: a body famous for leaping now shut behind casemate walls. The demagogue-hunt of the Karlsbad Decrees has found its most emblematic prisoner: the man who taught Germans to move, held motionless in a cell, while across the country the bars and beams of a hundred Turnplätze stand roped off and silent.

stops.name: Kolberg, the fortress by the Baltic
stops.campa: On 22 May 1820 Jahn is carried to the fortress of Kolberg on the Baltic, and there the long captivity grinds on. In 1823 his wife Helene dies, and he is not permitted to attend her funeral: the state denies the prisoner even his grief. He is tried, sentenced, the sentence quashed and renewed; his health frays behind the ramparts. For years the Turnvater sits by the cold sea, the freest of men in body made the most confined, paying with his own stillness for the movement he set loose upon Germany.

segments.name: Freyburg an der Unstrut: The Watched Old Age (1825–1852)

stops.name: Freyburg an der Unstrut, release under watch
stops.campa: On 15 March 1825 Jahn is freed at last, but on a leash: he may not live in any university or gymnasium town, and must report himself to the police. He settles in the little wine-town of Freyburg on the Unstrut, marries Emilie Hentsch, and builds a house there, a watched pensioner, forbidden his own life's work. Among the vineyards the caged Turnvater grows old, receiving pilgrims who steal to his door, the living monument of a banned movement, waiting out the fear of princes with the patience of stone.

stops.name: Kölleda, banished again
stops.campa: In September 1828 even Freyburg is denied him: because he keeps company with schoolboys of the district, Jahn is expelled to Kölleda on a charge of sedition, and there kept for years. When a Massachusetts college offers the famous old rebel a professor's chair across the ocean, he refuses with a hunter's grim wit: that deer and hares love best to live where they are most hunted. He will not flee the fatherland that hounds him. He waits it out, and only in 1836 is suffered to return to his house on the Unstrut.
stops.quote: Deer and hares love to live where they are most hunted.
stops.quote_source: Jahn, declining a professorship of German literature at Cambridge, Massachusetts (as recorded in Ripley & Dana, The American Cyclopædia, 1879)

stops.name: Freyburg, the pardon and the Iron Cross
stops.campa: In 1840 the new king Friedrich Wilhelm IV pardons the old demagogue and restores to him the Iron Cross he won at war in 1813. The Turnsperre is lifted; the bars and beams stand free again; a rising generation reveres the grey Turnvater as a founder. Rehabilitated in his own lifetime, Jahn walks the Freyburg vineyards a vindicated man. The movement no state could kill spreads now through German towns and, carried by emigrants, across the sea to the Turnvereine of the new world.

stops.name: Frankfurt, the Paulskirche: the deputy of 1848
stops.campa: In the revolution of 1848 the district of Naumburg sends the seventy-year-old Jahn to the German National Assembly in the Paulskirche at Frankfurt. He who dreamed the one free Germany takes his seat in the first parliament that dares to try to make it. Yet the old patriot sits with the right, cool to the republicans, and the younger gymnasts who wanted a people's revolution turn on him as too tame. The prophet outlives into an age his fire helped kindle, and finds the flame has run on past its keeper.

stops.name: Freyburg an der Unstrut, the Turnvater's grave
stops.campa: On 15 October 1852 Friedrich Ludwig Jahn dies at Freyburg on the Unstrut, aged seventy-four, almost unnoticed by the public of the day. He is laid in the earth of the town that both sheltered and confined him. But the movement outlives the man beyond all measure: over his grave a memorial gymnasium rises, monuments climb in Berlin's Hasenheide and across the German lands, and wherever Germans settle, the Turnverein carries frisch, fromm, fröhlich, frei. The body he made a fatherland outlasts every prince who feared it.
